title: ‘We will become cyborgs!’ Peter Gabriel on bonobo ape duets, building a Jurassic Park for plants – and why AI will make great music
summary:
From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas

Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles.

There has been a food media outcry, with a tone that has felt very “I’m not angry, I’m just disappointed”. According to the Observer report, “tonnes of mined rock salt are being poured into the production line” at Maldon. The scandal is that these brands call themselves sea salt (made by evaporating seawater), but rock salt is mined from dried-up underground seabeds (that were once also seas). Salt companies combine one type of salt with another to ultimately produce … salt. As food manufacturing goes, I don’t find it the most shocking transgression.

“Posh salt”, once marketed only to the upper classes in Harrods and Fortnums, has been gaining popularity over the last half century. In the early 00s, the major supermarkets started selling Maldon sea salt, and over the last 20 years, with the chef-ification of home cookery, flaky salt has reached never-before-seen heights.

title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial

The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another.

This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives.

title: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album
summary:

The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”.

A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre’s epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied. Released at the height of the 2020 Covid lockdown – when everyone was, by default, some distance from the dancefloor – his last album, Scacco Matto, expanded his palette to include lush ambient electronics, quasi-classical chord structures and something of the teeming chaos of Rustie’s digital maximalism.

Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. Z amplifies this heady feeling later on in Exit, Elsewhere, where her overlapping narration and rattling bells cause total disorientation.

title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
summary:
A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose

John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal.

Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his tastes run to the surprisingly sludgy. Orchids and roses have their place in the Green Kingdom, but nothing thrills him more than an evil-looking pond, rich in microscopic nutrients.

title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison

Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
summary:

  • Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
summary:
Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy

• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong.

For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear.

It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag.

Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. summary:

It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
summary:
IMMA, Dublin
From massacre locations painted on to basalt slabs to photocollages of bulldozed airports, artists from across the Levant address their traumatic history

In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.”

Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold.

The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of these (mostly) Palestinian artists also weaves a traumatic national history into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interlinked world in which we now live.

At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world.

At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in some of his religious paintings, including the Ghent altarpiece, these are the sum total of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.

It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness.
